```{r include=FALSE,echo=FALSE}
require(tigerstats)
require(tidyverse)
mydata <- read.csv(file="pushups.csv")
```

# Introduction

This report asks whether Georgetown College football players at line positions and skill positions have the same average number of push-ups. The data are the `pushups` dataset from the `tigerstats` package, supplied in this project as `pushups.csv`. Two players asked their teammates to do as many push-ups as they could in two minutes. There are 30 players. Each row records body weight in pounds, the number of push-ups completed, and position. Position has two categories: `LINE` (positions that require high body mass) and `SKILL` (positions that require a lot of running).

The question is a comparison of a numerical response, push-ups, across a categorical grouping variable, position. The hypotheses are:

$H_0$: There is no difference between the average number of pushups of line vs skill players.

$H_A$: The average number of pushups done by line players is statistically different than that of skill players.

# Methods

Position is categorical, with levels LINE and SKILL. The number of push-ups is numerical. This is a categorical-versus-numerical question with two groups, so the comparison of averages uses a two-sample *t*-test.

The descriptive part of the report has two pieces. A side-by-side boxplot shows the center and spread of push-ups in each position. A numerical summary gives the sample size, five-number summary, mean, and standard deviation for each group.

The inferential test is Welch's two-sample *t*-test of `pushups` by `position`. The alternative hypothesis is two-sided, because it says the averages are different and does not state which group is higher. Welch's test compares means and does not require the two groups to have the same variance. That choice fits these data: the groups are unequal in size, and the numerical summary shows that skill players are more spread out than line players. The significance level is 0.05.

The test treats the 30 players as independent observations. It also relies on the push-up counts within each position being roughly normal, or at least not so skewed that the mean is a poor summary. Those conditions are checked against the boxplot and the group sizes in the results.

# Results

## Descriptive Results

### Graphical Descriptive Results

The boxplot below compares the numerical push-up counts for the two position categories. Under the null hypothesis the two boxes would have similar centers. They do not. The skill box sits well above the line box, and the two boxes do not overlap. A typical skill player completed more push-ups in two minutes than a typical line player. Line players are packed into a low, narrow range. Skill players are higher and more spread out, including one very high value.

```{r}
boxplot(
  pushups ~ position,
  data = mydata,
  main = "Push-ups by football position",
  xlab = "Position",
  ylab = "Push-ups in two minutes",
  col = c("#9ecae1", "#a1d99b")
)
```

This graph is aimed at the hypothesis under test. It shows a large separation in the center of the push-up distribution, with skill players higher. That pattern is what a difference in averages would look like. The graph does not by itself give the probability of a difference this large if the null hypothesis were true. That probability comes from the *t*-test in the inferential section.
